title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why isn't the night sky blazing with light?
summary: A seemingly simple observation—that the sky is dark at night—turns out to be a profound clue about the size, age, and origin of the universe.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. The sky is mostly black, punctuated by a few thousand visible stars. This seems utterly unremarkable—until you consider the numbers. If the universe is infinite in extent and uniformly filled with stars, then in every direction you look, your line of sight should eventually hit a star's surface. The whole sky should blaze as brightly as the surface of the sun. It doesn't. This is Olbers' Paradox, named after the 19th-century astronomer Heinrich Olbers, though the puzzle was noted earlier by Johannes Kepler and Edmund Halley.

The Naive Argument

Imagine the universe as an infinite, static, evenly populated field of stars. As you look further out, you see more stars—the number of stars in a thin spherical shell around you grows with the square of the distance. But the brightness of each individual star falls off with the square of the distance too, by the inverse-square law. These two effects cancel out exactly, which means every shell of space, no matter how far away, contributes the same total amount of light to the sky. Add up infinitely many shells, and you get infinite brightness. Every point in the sky should eventually be covered by a star's disc, however distant, making the entire sky as luminous as a stellar surface.

Why the Sky Is Actually Dark

The resolution is not that starlight gets absorbed by dust—dust would simply heat up and re-radiate the energy, restoring the paradox. The real resolution is that the universe's simplifying assumptions are wrong. The universe is not infinitely old and static: it began roughly 13.8 billion years ago. Light from stars farther than about 13.8 billion light-years hasn't had time to reach us yet, which caps how many shells actually contribute. Even more importantly, the universe is expanding, so light from very distant, receding sources gets redshifted—stretched into longer, less energetic wavelengths, and much of the earliest light has been shifted all the way into the microwave band, which is precisely what we observe as the cosmic microwave background. Finally, stars are not eternal; they burn for a finite time, so distant, ancient regions of space may simply lack stars still shining at the moment their light was emitted.

A Paradox That Predicted Cosmology

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is that a simple observation anyone can make—look up, notice darkness—rules out an entire class of cosmological models: infinite, static, eternal universes uniformly filled with stars. Long before Hubble discovered cosmic expansion or Penzias and Wilson detected the microwave background, the dark night sky was already whispering that the universe must have a beginning, or be expanding, or both. It is a rare case where a piece of everyday, unaided-eye evidence constrains theories that otherwise require telescopes and particle accelerators to test.

perspectives.title: Astrophysics Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is resolved by a finite universe age (a light-travel-time horizon) combined with cosmological redshift diluting the energy of ancient starlight before it reaches us.

perspectives.title: Historical Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler used the dark sky as evidence for a finite universe as early as 1610; the puzzle sharpened over centuries as Newtonian infinite-universe models became popular, then was resolved only once Big Bang cosmology matured in the 20th century.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamics Perspective
perspectives.description: If starlight filled all of space uniformly, radiation and matter would reach thermal equilibrium at stellar temperatures—an outcome thermodynamically absurd given the universe's actual low background temperature of about 2.7 Kelvin.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox is a textbook case of a simple observation falsifying an entire family of theoretical models, illustrating how cosmology can be constrained by evidence available to anyone, not just specialists with instruments.
